items.prompt: Which word is an adverb? The snail moved slowly across the leaf.

options.why: This is a noun, the name of the animal.
This is a noun, the name of a thing.
This word shows position, it does not tell how the snail moved.

hints: An adverb tells more about a verb.
Ask: how did the snail move?
Find the word that answers how.
items.explanation: Slowly tells us how the snail moved, so it is an adverb.

hints: Ask whether the word tells how or when something happens.
"He walked ___" is how. "He walked ___ " can also fit time words.
Test each word in the sentence "She did it ___."
items.explanation: Quickly, carefully and loudly tell us how. Yesterday, soon and later tell us when.

items.prompt: Amara spoke ___ so the baby would not wake up.
hints: The missing word tells how she spoke.
It describes the verb, so it is an adverb.
Many adverbs end in -ly.
items.explanation: Quietly is an adverb that tells how Amara spoke. Quiet is an adjective.

items.prompt: Which part is an adverbial phrase? We ate lunch under the old banyan tree.

options.why: This is the subject and the verb.
This is the object, the thing that was eaten.
This is a single adjective inside the phrase.

hints: An adverbial phrase tells where, when or how.
Ask: where did they eat?
Find the group of words that answers where.
items.explanation: Under the old banyan tree tells where they ate, so it is an adverbial phrase.

items.prompt: Match each adverb to what it tells us.
hints: Ask what question each word answers.
Rarely tells how many times, not how.
Start with outside.
items.explanation: Carefully tells how, tomorrow tells when, outside tells where and rarely tells how often.

items.prompt: Write the adverb in this sentence. The cat crept silently towards the bird.
hints: The adverb tells how the cat crept.
Many adverbs end in -ly.
Find the word that describes the verb crept.
items.explanation: Silently tells how the cat crept, so it is the adverb.

items.answer: After the storm, the sky turned gold.
hints: The sentence begins with an adverbial phrase.
A comma follows the phrase at the start.
Start with After.
items.explanation: After the storm is a fronted adverbial phrase that tells when, and it is followed by a comma.

items.prompt: Which sentence has an adverb that tells how often?

options.why: Quickly tells how he ran.
Nearby tells where they live.
Early tells when the bus arrived.

hints: Look for a word about how many times.
Words like always, never and sometimes tell how often.
Which sentence is about repeating an action?
items.explanation: Sometimes tells us how often Rina walks to school.

items.prompt: Which adverb best shows the writer is unsure? ___ the train will be late, but we cannot be sure.

options.why: This shows the writer is certain.
This shows the writer is certain.
This shows the writer thinks it is clear.

hints: The sentence ends with "we cannot be sure".
Choose an adverb of possibility, not certainty.
Which word means maybe?
items.explanation: Perhaps means maybe, so it fits a sentence that says we cannot be sure.

hints: Ask: does the phrase answer when or where?
Time phrases often use days, meals or parts of the day.
Place phrases show a position or direction.
items.explanation: In the morning, after lunch and on Friday tell when. At the park, behind the shed and across the river tell where.

items.prompt: Write an adverb that means "in a happy way". The children sang ___.
hints: The word tells how they sang.
Take a describing word for happy and change it into an adverb.
Many adverbs end in -ly.
items.explanation: Adverbs such as happily or cheerfully tell how the children sang.

items.prompt: Turn each adjective into an adverb.
head: Adjective
Adverb
hints: Most adverbs add -ly, but some change first.
For words ending in y, change the y to i first.
For words ending in le, drop the e then add y.
items.explanation: Happy becomes happily, gentle becomes gently and easy becomes easily.

items.prompt: Which sentence punctuates the adverbial phrase correctly?

options.text: At the end of the lesson Mr Hadi, collected the books.
options.why: The comma splits the subject from the verb.

options.text: At the end, of the lesson Mr Hadi collected the books.
options.why: The comma splits the phrase in two.

options.text: At the end of the lesson Mr Hadi collected, the books.
options.why: The comma splits the verb from its object.

options.text: At the end of the lesson, Mr Hadi collected the books.

hints: The phrase comes at the start of the sentence.
A comma follows a fronted adverbial phrase.
Find the whole phrase, then put the comma straight after it.
items.explanation: The fronted phrase "At the end of the lesson" is followed by a comma before the main clause.

items.prompt: Choose all the sentences that contain an adverbial phrase, not just a single adverb.

options.text: We played football in the muddy field.

options.why: Happily is a single adverb, not a phrase.

options.text: Late at night, the owl hooted.

options.why: Quickly is a single adverb, not a phrase.

hints: A phrase has more than one word.
Look for groups of words that tell where, when or how long.
Cross out sentences where only one word does the job.
items.explanation: In the muddy field, late at night and for ten minutes are phrases. Happily and quickly are single adverbs.

items.prompt: Amara wrote in her diary: "Yesterday, we walked slowly through the market. Suddenly, a goat ran past us. In a flash it disappeared behind the stalls."

parts.prompt: Which phrase tells how quickly the goat disappeared?

options.why: This tells where the goat went.
This tells when it happened.
This tells where the goat ran.

parts.prompt: Write the adverb that tells how they walked.

hints: Ask how, when and where for each phrase.
"How quickly" asks about speed.
Look for words about speed or manner.
items.explanation: In a flash tells us how fast the goat went. Slowly tells how they walked.
